claim: In the abstract Wason selection task only about 4 to 10 percent choose the logical p and not-q cards. The modal choices are p+q (about 46%) and p alone (about 33%). The pattern holds across many experiments.
agent_test: Benchmark only: measure the plain model's abstract-task pass rate per model class before using any scaffold element (S0 class pass rate).

claim: Positive testing (choosing tests that fit your current hypothesis) is a default strategy, not a wish to confirm. It is a sound heuristic when the hypothesis is about as broad as the truth and the target is rare. It fails when the hypothesis is narrower than the truth, because then a yes answer can never expose the error.
agent_test: At equal tokens, compare an S4 rule 'include at least one test the hypothesis predicts will FAIL' against free test choice on rule-discovery items where the first guess is too narrow.

claim: People told their rule is wrong tend to keep it and reword it. In Wason 1960, 6 of 29 found the rule with no wrong announcement, 13 had one wrong, 9 had two or more, 1 never announced; subjects kept the same rule in over half the cases after being told it was wrong.
agent_test: S5 rule: a revision must change the predicted outcome on some concrete probe; measure how often the agent's revision is a rewording (code check: same predictions on a probe set).

claim: The information-gain model (Oaksford and Chater) fits card frequencies in 34 abstract-task studies (845 subjects, Spearman rho .92 on the 1994 subset) when p and q are assumed rare. Fits are by the model's authors with free parameters, and rivals fit comparably.
agent_test: Rank candidate tests by expected information gain computed in code (predicted split of the hypothesis set) and compare with model-chosen tests at equal tokens.

claim: Selections within one experiment depend on each other more than chance (99 of 228 experiments more redundant than simulated independent runs) and a salient counterexample raises its card's selection. The source is the proponent of model theory; critics say the model comparison is not identifiable.
agent_test: Not directly testable on the agent; only a reason to expect counterexample salience to matter (see A01.02-K07).

claim: Thematic content changes performance: permission and social-contract rules give 70 to 80 percent correct against 20 to 25 percent for matched descriptive rules (Cosmides). The effect replicates in weaker form (45 percent social contract vs 15 percent control, Fiddick) and its cause is disputed (social-exchange module, pragmatic schemas, relevance, deontic framing).
agent_test: Test O6 (change representation): rewrite an abstract rule as a concrete 'who breaks the rule?' question; compare at equal tokens; code scores p and not-q selection.

claim: Making the contrast explicit helps humans on the 2-4-6 task. The dual-goal (DAX/MED) version raises success from about 20 percent to over 60 percent (Gale and Ball 2006, abstract read). Thinking in opposites gave 78 percent against 37 percent in controls (N=180). Numbers for the opposites study were re-read (N = 180, 78.33 vs 38.33 vs 36.66 percent). No independent replication of it was found; Rossi 2001 and Gale and Ball 2012 figures are known only through Branchini.
agent_test: Add a contrast step to S2: for each candidate rule write its complement and one triple that should satisfy the complement; compare with no contrast step at equal tokens.

claim: Listing properties of the seed example without building opposites did nothing (38 percent vs 37 percent control). The contrast must be along the dimension that matters; a wrong-dimension contrast example gave only about 20 to 34 percent (second-hand).
agent_test: In the A01.02-K07 ablation add a wrong-dimension contrast arm to check that the agent needs the right one.

claim: In LLM rule-discovery games the share of tests that could falsify the current guess correlates with success. Success ranges 6 to 78 percent across 11 models (Jhaveri) and positive-test share vs success has rho -0.78 across 12 models (Bertolazzi). Correlational, not causal.
agent_test: Log falsifying-test share per run and check that it predicts success for our agent; then intervene by forcing it (A01.02-K02).

claim: Reasoning (thinking) models do better at rule discovery and falsify more: GPT-5.2-Chat 75 percent and GPT-OSS-120B 68 percent vs 33 to 41 percent for instruction-tuned (FalsifyBench); Gemini-2.5-Pro 0.73 vs 0.06 to 0.33 for small non-thinking models (Jhaveri); on WILT the best model solves only 14 of 50.
agent_test: Gains are model-class dependent. Check that scaffold elements help non-thinking and thinking models alike before assuming they transfer.

claim: A prompt telling the LLM to pick one property of its last test and test the opposite (Think-in-Opposites) did not lower success in any of 11 model settings (equal in Qwen3-8B non-thinking, 0.062 before and after). Averaged over episodes it raised success by +0.123 for thinking models and +0.063 for non-thinking models, both significant. Only thinking models raised their share of falsifying tests significantly. Dual-Goal helped thinking models (+0.148) and hurt non-thinking ones (-0.060, p = 0.0065). Thinking-model tokens per turn rose by about 12 to 58 percent with TiO, and no token-matched control was run.
agent_test: Replicate TiO vs plain at equal tokens on our agent with 80 or more episodes per arm.

claim: Part of the LLM gain comes from choosing tests well rather than inferring the rule: o1-mini given chatgpt-4o-latest's tests guessed 19 of 50 rules, above the best single-model full run (14 of 50), and the text says it did worse with its own tests (the number is only in a figure). So the evidence points to a stronger-tester effect. A role split on one model, with the same model playing both roles, has not been tested at matched tokens. Weak models also repeat tests (GPT-4o-mini about 9.8 repeats per rule).
agent_test: Split test proposal from rule inference (inferer sees only outcomes, G3) and compare with one combined call at equal tokens. Code blocks duplicate tests.

claim: LLMs show the human content effect on the Wason task: realistic rules beat arbitrary ones (Chinchilla, PaLM 2-L, GPT-3.5 and humans, all z>2.2). Small open models mostly fail the standard form (0.06 to 0.29, chance 1/6). The social-rule advantage is weak or absent in LLMs in one study.
agent_test: Check agent accuracy on matched abstract vs concrete rules; if the gap is big, add a concrete re-expression step (A01.02-K06).

claim: On deontic Wason problems LLM errors fit matching bias better than confirmation bias. Reasoning models reach 98 to 100 percent zero-shot (gpt-oss-120b 100.0, qwen3-32b 98.8) while small models are low (gemma3-4b 17.5). Chain of thought hurt gemma3-12b (few-shot 78.7 to 43.8) but helped llama-3.3-70b (83.8).
agent_test: Longer reasoning can hurt weak models; test short vs long reasoning per model class on the selection task.

claim: Scoring candidate questions by expected information gain in code, with the LLM only proposing candidates, raises success: +37.4 points on 20 Questions (Choudhury 2026), Llama-4-Scout Battleship win rate 8 to 82 percent (Grand 2026), and hypothesis-set approaches beat direct LLM proposal in Zendo-like tasks (Piriyakulkij 2024). Caveat: when the same LLM also generates the hypothesis set (Gemini 2.5 Flash, number game), EIG query choice was no better than random on easy rules and failed on hard ones where the generator never proposes the true rule (Chari and Pattanaik 2026).
agent_test: Code scores candidate tests by expected split of the hypothesis set; compare with the model picking its own test at equal tokens.

claim: Sequential falsification tests under a Type-I error budget (POPPER) gave power 0.61 vs 0.38 for ReAct on DiscoveryBench at Type-I 0.1; a relevance checker was needed to keep Type-I control.
agent_test: Relevant to open scientific-hypothesis tasks only, not ARC-type items.

claim: Confirmatory test preference persists in trained people: Dutch judges 22.2 percent correct on the abstract task and 40 percent chose confirming options only; maths majors and mathematicians below 50 percent on arbitrary rules; confirmatory question preference in social interviews (Swann and Giuliano).
agent_test: Not an agent test. Reason not to trust the agent's own 'I checked it' (supports G10).

claim: Tutoring on the selection task gives modest task-specific gains (Osman 2007: logical choices about 37 to 66 percent in one experiment, read from a garbled table). Transfer is not shown.
agent_test: Test S9 lesson lines for transfer to a differently worded item of the same class, not the same item.

claim: Matching bias (choosing cards named in the rule) explains much of abstract selection-task choice: about 75 percent of data fit an inference submodel and 25 percent guessing in one model fit. Whether it is a shallow heuristic or a relevance effect is disputed; negated-consequent versions reach about 60 percent correct.
agent_test: Probe the agent with negated-consequent variants of each rule; accuracy tied to wording means it matches surface tokens.

claim: Chain-of-thought length is not a safe lever for hypothesis work. On deontic Wason problems zero-shot CoT raised llama-3.3-70b from 62.5 to 83.8 and olmo-2-32b from 36.2 to 57.5 but lowered gemma3-12b from 58.8 to 43.8 and gemma3-27b from 77.5 to 62.5. On other induction and implicit-learning tasks CoT lowered accuracy by up to 36 points for o1-preview. No controlled test exists on rule discovery with chosen tests.
agent_test: Run the agent with a short and a long thinking budget on the same rule set, 80 or more episodes per arm and per model, and keep the winner per model.

claim: The bottleneck in LLM rule induction is generating the right hypothesis, not checking or refining it. Refinement rescued 4.3 percent of semantically wrong hypotheses (GPT-4o, 5,500 trials). EIG query choice cannot fix a generator that never proposes the true rule. Exploration breadth (5 independent explorers) beat refinement on ARC-AGI-1 (N=1 never above 45.5 percent, N=5 reached 57.5 percent pass@2).
agent_test: Compare k independent hypothesis sets against one set refined k times at equal tokens; count how often the winning hypothesis changes predictions.

claim: Separate exploration from synthesis and re-explore when the current program fails. On ARC-AGI-1 with non-thinking DeepSeek V3.2: structured CoT 30.0, explorer-definer pipeline 57.5, reflective orchestrator 67.25 percent pass@2. Cost rose to 125x and 310x the one-shot baseline, so this is not token-matched. The orchestrator lift was +6.06 on Qwen3-235B with a CI including zero.
agent_test: Rerun with a token-matched best-of-n CoT arm before trusting the structural gain.

claim: LLM first hypotheses are too narrow by default (strong-sampling assumption, implicit Occam's razor), and thinking mode moves them toward the prior. This is the case where only a test outside the hypothesis can falsify it. Judging a given rule is easier for the model than generating one.
agent_test: Count how often the first guess is a strict subset of the true rule in our task classes; if high, always include one test outside the guess.

claim: Whether a revised hypothesis is only a rewording has not been measured for current LLMs. The measurable parts exist: exact repeated tests (up to 9.8 per rule for weak models), per-turn labelling of hypothesis versus target (FalsifyBench), and entity-level versus text-level change (Tiny Moves).
agent_test: In code, run old and new hypothesis on the same held-out inputs; a revision that changes no prediction counts as a rewording and is rejected.

claim: No study was found that compares a code-enforced falsifying-test rule against the same rule in the prompt, at matched tokens, for thinking and non-thinking models. Same for the human-debiasing effect: the opposites result (N=180) has no independent replication found.
agent_test: Three arms at matched tokens: plain, prompt-only falsify, code-gated falsify (code rejects any round whose tests all fit the current hypothesis).
